strengths: Strong motivation grounded in spectral analysis: The paper presents a solid analysis of the spectral dynamics of the reverse diffusion process, showing that low-frequency structures converge early, while high-frequency details resolve throughout the denoising process.

Training-free and lightweight: DYPE is a training-free plug-and-play method that introduces no additional training or inference overhead, making it highly practical for adapting pre-trained DiTs (such as FLUX) to ultra-high resolutions.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated on both text-to-image and class-conditional generation across various resolutions (up to 4096 x 4096 and higher), with both automated metrics and human preference studies showing a clear advantage (approx. 87-90% preference rate over static counterparts).
Detailed ablation studies: The appendix provides a thorough exploration of the hyperparameter space and scheduler designs, helping to justify the chosen design configurations.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to hyperparameters: The method introduces several hyperparameters ($\lambda_s$, $\lambda_t$, etc.). While ablated, the optimal choice of these parameters could vary across different models (e.g., FLUX vs. FiTv2), step counts, and noise schedules, requiring some manual tuning.

Minor presentation/placeholder issues: There are placeholder citations in the paper (e.g., 'YourTeam, 2025' in Section 1 and 'Placeholder YourTeam. Fit v2...' in the references on Page 15) which should be cleaned up for the camera-ready version.

strengths: Strong Motivation & Solid Grounding: The paper elegantly connects the spectral progression of the diffusion process (where low-frequency global structures converge early, and high-frequency details are resolved late) with the design of dynamic positional encoding interpolation, providing a solid mathematical and intuitive justification.

Completely Training-Free & Highly Practical: The proposed DYPE method requires no retraining, introduces no additional parameters, and incurs zero computational or inference overhead, making it highly practical for scaling existing pre-trained DiT models (such as FLUX) to ultra-high resolutions.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The authors present thorough quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The method is validated on multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet) using a wide suite of metrics (CLIPScore, ImageReward, Aesthetic Score, FID, sFID, IS, and human preference), demonstrating consistent and significant improvements.

Impressive Qualitative Quality: DYPE is shown to generate highly coherent, ultra-high-resolution images (up to 4096 x 4096 and 16M+ pixels) without the repetitive patterns and artifacts that commonly plague standard baseline models and static positional interpolation strategies.

Clear Presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, well-structured, and easy to follow. The explanation of the frequency analysis (Fig. 2) and the detailed progression from static to dynamic PE formulations are exemplary.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter Tuning Dependency: DYPE introduces additional hyperparameters ($\lambda_s$ and $\lambda_t$) for the time-dependent scheduler $\kappa(t)$. Although the ablation study in the appendix demonstrates good choices, there is limited discussion on how sensitive the generation quality is to these parameters across widely different aspect ratios or entirely different model architectures.

Inherent Quadratic Complexity of Attention: While DYPE itself has no additional sampling cost, generating ultra-high-resolution images (e.g., 4096^2) with DiTs still suffers from the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. A brief discussion on the practical memory/latency trade-offs of running DiTs at these scales (even with DYPE) would provide better context for real-world deployment.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely topic: training-free ultra-high-resolution image generation for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs).
The core idea of leveraging the spectral progression of diffusion (low-to-high frequency convergence) to dynamically adjust positional interpolation is intuitive and physically well-motivated.
The proposed formulation is versatile and can be seamlessly integrated into existing positional encoding extrapolation methods (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN).
Qualitative results show notable improvements in reducing structural repetitions and preserving fine-grained details compared to standard static baselines.
weaknesses: Flawed Metric Evaluation: The FID scores on Aesthetic-4K in Table 1 are computed using only 195 curated image-prompt pairs. Calculating FID on such a small sample size is highly statistically unstable and scientifically unreliable, as FID typically requires thousands of samples to yield meaningful estimates. This makes the quantitative FID claims unconvincing.

Conceptual Misunderstanding of Training Conditions: In Section 3.1, the authors state that turning off scaling at $t \approx 0$ allows the denoiser to operate in the PE conditions it was trained with. This is mathematically incorrect. For a $4096 \times 4096$ image, the token coordinate range is much larger than the $1024 \times 1024$ training range. Without scaling, the relative distances in RoPE exceed 1024, exposing the self-attention layers to completely out-of-distribution phase shifts that the model never encountered during training. The paper lacks a rigorous analysis of why the model is robust to these out-of-distribution inputs at later timesteps.

Heuristic Hyperparameter Scaling: The dynamic scaling function uses fixed hyperparameters $\lambda_s = \lambda_t = 2$ across all experiments. It is theoretically unclear why a fixed maximum scale $\lambda_s = 2$ is optimal regardless of whether the target resolution scale factor $s$ is 2 (for $2048^2$) or 6 (for $6144^2$). A systematic study of hyperparameter sensitivity with respect to target resolution is missing.

Unaddressed Inference Overhead: Unlike static extrapolation methods where RoPE embeddings can be computed once and cached, DYPE requires recomputing the RoPE trigonometric tables at every single diffusion step because $\kappa(t)$ changes. Although likely small compared to the heavy attention mechanism of FLUX, the paper claims 'no inference overhead' without providing wall-clock time measurements to support this.

Limited Baselines: The comparison is mostly confined to static PE methods and Lumina-Next. Comparing against other training-free resolution scaling methods (e.g., scale-fusion or patch-based approaches) adapted to DiTs would better contextualize the performance gains of PE-only modulation.

strengths: Well-founded motivation: The paper leverages the spectral dynamics of the diffusion process (where low-frequency structures converge early, while high-frequency details emerge later) to dynamically adjust positional encodings.

Training-free and lightweight: The proposed method (DyPE) requires no retraining or additional inference-time overhead, making it highly practical for adapting pretrained diffusion transformers to ultra-high resolutions.

Broad applicability and generalizability: The authors validate DyPE across several state-of-the-art models (FLUX, FiTv2, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1) and across multiple tasks (text-to-image, class-conditional generation, image editing, video generation, and panoramic synthesis).

Extensive evaluation: Quantitative results (using CLIPScore, ImageReward, FID, patch-FID, and human studies) show consistent improvements over baseline models and static position extrapolation techniques. The inclusion of attention entropy analysis provides deeper insights into why the method succeeds.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter dependency: The scaling scheduler κ(t) introduces hyperparameters (λs and λt) that may require tuning for different architectures or resolution scale factors, potentially affecting ease of deployment.

Hardware limitations at extreme scales: Although DyPE addresses the representation capacity of the positional encodings at high resolutions, it does not alleviate the native quadratic complexity of self-attention. Generating images at extreme resolutions (e.g., 4K and beyond) still requires substantial hardware memory, which may limit practical accessibility.

strengths: Well-motivated concept: The core idea of dynamically adjusting positional embeddings based on the spectral progression of the reverse diffusion process (coarse-to-fine structure generation) is theoretically elegant and practically sensible.
Training-free with zero overhead: The proposed method is plug-and-play and does not introduce additional computational or memory overhead during inference, making it highly practical.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors validate DyPE across several strong baseline models (FLUX, FiTv2, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1) and tasks (text-to-image, class-conditional, video generation, image editing). They include a rich set of metrics (FID, Patch-FID, ImageReward, CLIPScore, IS) and a human perceptual study.
Clarity and presentation: The paper is well-structured and easy to follow. The Fourier analysis of the diffusion process (Section 3.1) and visual examples are clear and highly informative.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter sensitivity: The dynamic scaling function introduces hyperparameters (lambda_s and lambda_t). While the authors provide ablations in the appendix, it remains slightly unclear how robust these hyperparameters are across different resolutions (e.g., scaling from 2K to 4K to 6K) or different model architectures, and whether significant tuning is needed for new settings.

Discussion on extreme resolutions: The scaling analysis in Figure 5 indicates a sharp drop in ImageReward at 6144x6144 resolution for both YaRN and DY-YaRN. A brief discussion on the physical limits of the proposed training-free extrapolation approach (e.g., context window limits or attention entropy collapse at extremely large scales) would benefit the paper's completeness.

strengths: Solid theoretical and empirical motivation: The paper provides a clear Fourier-space analysis of the spectral progression in the diffusion process, showing that low frequencies converge early while high frequencies resolve throughout sampling. This serves as a principled foundation for dynamic positional extrapolation.

Training-free and zero-overhead: The proposed DyPE is an inference-time adaptation that does not require retraining or fine-tuning, and introduces no computational or memory overhead during the generation process.

Excellent versatility: The method is shown to be highly generalizable, successfully enhancing multiple architectures (FLUX, Qwen-Image, FiTv2, and Wan2.1 video model) across various tasks (text-to-image, class-conditional generation, high-resolution editing, panoramas, and video generation).

Comprehensive evaluation: The authors conduct thorough quantitative evaluations (using CLIPScore, ImageReward, Aesthetic-Score, FID, patch-FID) and qualitative user studies, showing significant improvements over static PE baselines.
weaknesses: Heuristic scheduler formulation: Although the motivation from spectral dynamics is rigorous, the time-dependent scaling function is modeled via a simple heuristic power-law scheduler. A theoretical or more automated derivation of the optimal schedule based on the diffusion formulation would strengthen the work.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and tuning: The optimal hyperparameters are empirically set to lambda_s = 2 and lambda_t = 2. It is not fully clear how sensitive the generation quality is to these parameters across different resolutions and whether they require tedious manual tuning when applied to new, unseen models.

The inherent hardware bottleneck remains: While DyPE effectively resolves the positional representation issues for ultra-high-resolution generation, the quadratic attention complexity of Diffusion Transformers still limits practical scaling due to memory constraints. The paper would benefit from discussing how DyPE interacts with sequence-parallelism or memory-efficient attention techniques.
